analysis.one_liner: Adds a voluntary Medicare prescription drug benefit with the government negotiating drug prices directly.
analysis.headline: A Medicare drug benefit bill backed by 132 House cosponsors never received a committee vote and expired when the 108th Congress ended; a different drug benefit passed later that year without the price-negotiation provision.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added a voluntary prescription drug benefit to Medicare: enrollees would pay a $25 monthly premium, a $100 yearly deductible, and 20 percent coinsurance, with total out-of-pocket drug costs capped at $2,000 a year. Unlike the law Congress ultimately passed, the Secretary of Health and Human Services would have negotiated maximum prices with drug manufacturers, and the bill would have sped up generic drug competition. It was referred to two House committees in March 2003 and never came back.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially those with high drug costs, would gain guaranteed access to discounted prescription medicines with a hard $2,000 annual out-of-pocket cap. Employers keeping retiree drug coverage and generic drug makers would also gain.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries with high drug costs

how_it_helps.text: Every Medicare beneficiary would be entitled to enroll in a voluntary drug benefit with a $25 monthly premium, a $100 annual deductible, 20 percent coinsurance, and a $2,000 annual out-of-pocket limit, after which coverage is fully free of cost-sharing.

The Secretary of Health and Human Services would be required to negotiate contracts with drug manufacturers setting maximum prices for covered medicines, with pharmacy contractors required to negotiate even lower prices and pass the reductions to beneficiaries.
The bill provides for accelerated generic drug competition, which would bring cheaper versions of medicines to market sooner.
Transitional assistance is provided for low-income beneficiaries, and employers that continue retiree drug coverage would receive federal payments to keep those plans alive.
The bill includes guaranteed access rules for rural and hard-to-serve areas, bonus payments for rural pharmacists, and appeal rights when a preferred medicine does not work for a patient.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the new trust fund through appropriations beyond what premiums and cost-sharing cover, and brand-name drug manufacturers would earn less as negotiated maximum prices and faster generic competition cut into their pricing power.

drawbacks.text: Enrollees would still bear meaningful costs: a $25 monthly premium, a $100 annual deductible, and 20 percent coinsurance before the cap kicks in.
The bill creates a new trust fund financed by federal appropriations with no dedicated funding stream, so the benefit would add substantially to federal spending on top of beneficiary premiums.

Government-set maximum prices and accelerated generic entry would reduce brand-name drug manufacturers' revenue, which in a good-faith objection could slow investment in developing new medicines; the bill tries to soften this by directing negotiators to account for promoting breakthrough medicines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit design is unusually protective of patients: a $2,000 annual out-of-pocket cap with no coverage gap, plus direct government price negotiation. The real cost is fiscal — a large new federal entitlement funded by appropriations — and the risk, argued by drug makers, that negotiated price caps could modestly discourage development of some new medicines. On balance the bill traded industry revenue for strong patient protections and federal cost control.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees in March 2003 and then to their health subcommittees, where it sat; neither committee ever reported it, no vote was ever taken, and it expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Rangel introduced the bill on March 11, 2003, joined by Reps. Dingell, Stark, Waxman, Brown, Pallone and more than 100 other House members as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction.
In late March 2003 it was referred to the Health subcommittees of both committees; no further action was ever recorded.
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or support from a single Republican cosponsor among its 132 cosponsors.
Congress did enact a Medicare prescription drug benefit later in 2003, but under a different design that relied on private plans rather than government-negotiated maximum prices.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: later in 2003 Congress created the Medicare Part D benefit through private insurance plans and included a provision barring the government from negotiating drug prices, so manufacturers kept market-rate pricing. Private insurers and pharmacy middlemen gained the administering role that this bill would have kept largely inside Medicare with price caps.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and private plans

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the party's House leadership.

against.what_they_did: Chaired one of the two committees of referral and never reported the bill; instead shepherded the Republican-written drug benefit bill that Congress passed later in 2003.

sides.party_line_note: All 132 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run committees never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have let the government negotiate maximum prices for Medicare-covered drugs and accelerated generic competition, directly cutting into manufacturers' pricing power. The drug benefit Congress actually passed later in 2003 barred government negotiation, preserving their market-rate prices.

The bill routes the drug benefit through competitively bid pharmacy contractors, giving them a guaranteed administrative role, but caps what they can charge and holds their fees hostage to price-reduction and quality performance. It locks in their role while strictly regulating it.
Accelerated generic competition and required generic substitutes in each therapeutic class would expand their market, and cheaper generics lower costs for patients.

Pharmacies would get guaranteed participation rights, rural bonus payments, and dispensing fees, but would have to honor negotiated maximum prices and submit to audits. Rural and independent pharmacies come out comparatively well.
Medicare+Choice plans would be required to offer drug coverage but would receive added federal payments for it, with cost-sharing capped at the standard benefit's level.
